Document Name: MuJoCo
Document URL: https://mujoco.readthedocs.io/en/stable/_modules/mujoco_warp/_src/render_util.html
Document content:

MuJoCo’s runtime performs zero memory allocations after initialization – all working memory is preallocated in`mjData`. A single simulation step is single-threaded by default, but constraint islands enable per-island parallelism within a step. Large-scale data-parallel sampling is achieved by creating multiple `mjData`instances that share the same `mjModel` and running them on separate threads; see multi-threading.

Interactive simulation and visualization

The native 3D visualizer provides rendering of meshes and geometric primitives, textures, reflections, shadows, fog, transparency, wireframes, skyboxes, stereoscopic visualization (on video cards supporting quad-buffered OpenGL). This functionality is used to generate 3D rendering that helps the user gain insight into the physics simulation, including visual aids such as automatically generated model skeletons, equivalent inertia boxes, contact positions and normals, contact forces that can be separated into normal and tangential components, external perturbation forces, local frames, joint and actuator axes, and text labels. The visualizer expects a generic window with an OpenGL rendering context, thereby allowing users to adopt a GUI library of their choice. The code samplesimulate.cc distributed with MuJoCo shows how to do that with the GLFW library. A related usability feature is the ability to “reach into” the simulation, push objects around and see how the physics respond. The user selects the body to which the external forces and torques will be applied, and sees a real-time rendering of the perturbations together with their dynamic consequences. This can be used to debug the model visually, to test the response of a feedback controller, or to configure the model into a desired pose.

Powerful yet intuitive modeling language

MuJoCo has its own modeling language called MJCF. The goal of MJCF is to provide access to all of MuJoCo’s compute capabilities, and at the same time enable users to develop new models quickly and experiment with them. This goal is achieved in large part due to an extensive default setting mechanism that resembles Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) inlined in HTML. While MJCF has many elements and attributes, the user needs to set surprisingly few of them in any given model. This makes MJCF files shorter and more readable than many other formats.

Automated generation of composite flexible objects

MuJoCo’s soft constraints can be used to model ropes, cloth, and deformable 3D objects. This requires a large collection of regular bodies, joint, tendons and constraints to work together. Document Name: MuJoCo
Document URL: https://mujoco.readthedocs.io/en/stable/_modules/mujoco_warp/_src/support.html
Document content:
Overview#

## Introduction#

**MuJoCo** stands for **Mu**lti-**Jo**int dynamics with **Co**ntact. It is a general purpose physics engine that aims to facilitate research and development in robotics, biomechanics, graphics and animation, machine learning, and other areas that demand fast and accurate simulation of articulated structures interacting with their environment. Initially developed by Roboti LLC, it was acquired and made freely available by DeepMind in October 2021, and open sourced in May 2022\. The MuJoCo codebase is available at the google-deepmind/mujoco repository on GitHub.

MuJoCo is a C/C++ library with a C API, intended for researchers and developers. The runtime simulation module is tuned to maximize performance and operates on low-level data structures which are preallocated by the built-in XML parser and compiler. The user defines models in the native MJCF scene description language – an XML file format designed to be as human readable and editable as possible. URDF model files can also be loaded. The library includes interactive visualization with a native GUI, rendered in OpenGL. MuJoCo further exposes a large number of utility functions for computing physics-related quantities.

MuJoCo can be used to implement model-based computations such as control synthesis, state estimation, system identification, mechanism design, data analysis through inverse dynamics, and parallel sampling for machine learning applications. It can also be used as a more traditional simulator, including for gaming and interactive virtual environments.

____

Document Name: MuJoCo
Document URL: https://mujoco.readthedocs.io/en/stable/OpenUSD/mjcf_file_format_plugin.html
Document content:
## Usage#

1. **Installation:** refer to Building.
2. **Referencing in a USD file (e.g., \`\`.usda\`\`):**  
example.usda#  
#usda 1.0  
(  
    upAxis = "Z"  
)  
def Xform "world"  
{  
    def "robot" (  
        prepend references = @./my_robot.xml@  
    )  
    {  
    }  
}  
Copy to clipboard  
In this example, `my_robot.xml` is an MJCF file in the same directory. USD will use the plugin to load and interpret its contents.
3. **Opening in usdview:**  
usdview my_robot.xml  
Copy to clipboard  
If the plugin is correctly set up, `usdview` will render the robot defined in the MJCF file.
4. **Using in Python (with USD API):**  
from pxr import Usd  
# Load an MJCF file as a USD stage  
stage = Usd.Stage.Open('my_robot.xml')  
if stage:  
    print(f"Successfully opened {stage.GetRootLayer().identifier}")  
    # You can now inspect the stage as any other USD stage  
    for prim in stage.TraverseAll():  
        print(prim.GetPath())  
else:  
    print("Failed to open MJCF file")  
Copy to clipboard  
This plugin significantly enhances the interoperability between MuJoCo and USD-based workflows, allowing seamless integration of physics assets defined in MJCF into broader 3D environments

Document Name: MuJoCo
Document URL: https://mujoco.readthedocs.io/en/stable/_modules/mujoco_warp/_src/support.html
Document content:

This model is a 7 degree-of-freedom arm “holding” a string with a cylinder attached at the other end. The string is implemented as a tendon with length limits. There is ball joint at the shoulder and pairs of hinge joints at the elbow and wrist. The box inside the cylinder indicates a free “joint”. The outer body element in the XML is the requiredworldbody. Note that using multiple joints between two bodies does not require creating dummy bodies.

The MJCF file contains the minimum information needed to specify the model. Capsules are defined by line-segments in space – in which case only the radius of the capsule is needed. The positions and orientations of body frames are inferred from the geoms belonging to them. Inertial properties are inferred from the geom shape under a uniform density assumption. The two sites are named because the tendon definition needs to reference them, but nothing else is named. Joint axes are defined only for the hinge joints but not the ball joint. Collision rules are defined automatically. Friction properties, gravity, simulation time step etc. are set to their defaults. The default geom color specified at the top applies to all geoms.

Apart from saving the compiled model in the binary MJB format, we can save it as MJCF or as human-readable text; seeexample\_saved.xml and example\_saved.txtrespectively. The XML version is similar to the original, while the text version contains all information from`mjModel`. Comparing the text version to the XML version reveals how much work the model compiler did for us.

@MuJoCo Documentation This tool is used to export assemblies/parts from Solidworks CAD program to URDF for integration in simulation/robotics applications.  Update this tool to support exporting to the MuJoCo MJCF format, which is a richer XML-based format with support for additional features.
</user_query>
I need to understand how the current URDF export system works before I can add MJCF support, so I'm starting by exploring the codebase structure.
I should look at the UI to see how the export feature is actually triggered and what configuration options users have available.

I've explored the codebase. Here's what I found:

**Current architecture:**
- URDF model classes in [SW2URDF/URDF/](SW2URDF/URDF/) form a tree of `URDFElement` nodes. Each node serializes itself through `WriteURDF(XmlWriter)` (see [SW2URDF/URDF/URDFElement.cs](SW2URDF/URDF/URDFElement.cs) and [SW2URDF/URDF/Robot.cs](SW2URDF/URDF/Robot.cs)).
- Export orchestration lives in [SW2URDF/URDFExport/ExportHelper.cs](SW2URDF/URDFExport/ExportHelper.cs) (`ExportRobot`), which builds a ROS package (dirs, `CMakeLists.txt`, `package.xml`, RViz/Gazebo launchers), exports per-link meshes (STL or 3DXML via `MeshExportFormat` enum in [SW2URDF/URDFExport/ExportHelperExtension.cs](SW2URDF/URDFExport/ExportHelperExtension.cs)), then writes a single `.urdf`.
- UI: [SW2URDF/UI/AssemblyExportForm.Designer.cs](SW2URDF/UI/AssemblyExportForm.Designer.cs) has a `Mesh Format` group with `radioButtonStl` and `radioButton3dxml`; `FinishExport` in [SW2URDF/UI/AssemblyExportForm.cs](SW2URDF/UI/AssemblyExportForm.cs) chooses which to pass to `ExportRobot`.

**Key conceptual differences between URDF and MJCF** that affect the design:
- MJCF has a top-level `<mujoco>` with `<compiler>`, `<option>`, `<default>`, `<asset>`, `<worldbody>`, (optionally `<actuator>`, `<sensor>`, `<contact>`).
- Bodies are **nested** (child `<body>` inside parent `<body>`), not flat like URDF's `<link>`+`<joint>` pairs.
- `<joint>` lives inside the child `<body>`; types map `revolute/continuous → hinge`, `prismatic → slide`, `fixed → <body>` without a joint, `floating → free`.
- Meshes go in `<asset><mesh .../></asset>` and are referenced by name from `<geom type="mesh" mesh="..."/>`. Visual vs. collision is expressed via `group`/`contype`/`conaffinity`.
- Orientations use `euler` or `quat`; units match URDF (meters, kg, radians).
- **MuJoCo does not load 3DXML meshes** - only STL/OBJ/MSH. 3DXML would not be a valid mesh format for MJCF.

Before I draft a plan, I need to clarify a few things:

 I'm getting a clearer picture of the structure now—looking at how Inertia, Mass, Mesh, Visual, and Collision components map to MJCF format. I should also check the examples and ROSFiles.cs to see what ROS-specific packaging details I'd need to filter out when converting to MJCF. The URDF model classes in the SW2URDF directory seem to form the core of what I'm working with.

The key differences between URDF and MJCF are significant: MJCF uses a nested body hierarchy within the XML rather than flat link-joint pairs, replaces separate visual and collision elements with a single geom element, stores inertial properties as compact attributes, and places joints as children of bodies with different type names. Meshes are centralized in an asset section and referenced by geometry elements.

Before I can create a solid implementation plan, I need to clarify a few design decisions with the user. First, should MJCF be offered as an additional export format alongside URDF, replace URDF entirely, or always be generated in parallel? Second, since MuJoCo doesn't support 3DXML, should we restrict MJCF exports to STL meshes or add OBJ support as well? Third, for the output structure, should we maintain the existing ROS package layout with the MJCF file added, or create a simpler MuJoCo-specific directory structure? And finally, which MJCF-specific features like actuators, sensors, and contact properties should we prioritize supporting in this initial implementation?

The user is looking for full MJCF support with actuators, equality constraints, contact exclusions, and exposed configuration options—features that URDF doesn't handle well. I'm leaning toward adding a separate "Export MJCF..." button to keep the URDF export clean while giving MJCF its own dedicated flow with those advanced features.

The key insight is that we can reuse the same link/joint tree that users build in the assembly form, then branch at export time: they choose either "Export URDF" or "Export MJCF..." which opens a dialog for MJCF-specific settings like gravity, timestep, integrator, and actuator configuration. Rather than mirroring the entire URDF element hierarchy for MJCF, I think a single `MjcfWriter` class that consumes the existing `Robot` tree and directly outputs MJCF XML is the cleanest approach—it avoids duplication while handling the structural differences between URDF's flat links/joints and MuJoCo's nested body hierarchy. Now I'm wondering about mesh file handling and how paths should be resolved in the MJCF output.

I'll keep it simple: reuse the same `meshes/` directory and set the `meshdir` relative to the MJCF file location. Before I finalize the full plan, I should check how the existing `Inertia` and `Mesh` classes handle axis conventions to make sure the translation is correct.

Good - I have enough to draft a solid plan. Based on your input, I'll go with the dedicated **Export MJCF…** button path (clean separation, room to expose MJCF-specific options), full feature scope (actuators, mimic → `<equality>`, contact excludes, compiler/option controls), reuse the existing `Robot` tree as the intermediate representation, and emit a separate `MjcfWriter` that translates it.

Should we add sensors, cameras, lights, and sites now?
</user_query>

Good question — it's worth deciding before I start building. Here's my take on the trade-offs:

**Why I put them out of scope initially:**
- None of them have a source in the current `Robot` / `Link` / `Joint` model or in the SolidWorks assembly concepts the tool already inspects.
- Supporting them properly (so they survive the CSV round-trip in [SW2URDF/URDFExport/CSV/](SW2URDF/URDFExport/CSV/) and the `DataContract` serializers) means extending the URDF element hierarchy and adding UI surface — a notable expansion beyond translating what's already captured.
- Users typically hand-tune sensors/cameras/lights for their simulation task and will often edit the exported MJCF regardless.

**However, two of them are genuinely cheap to add now and add real value:**
- A single default `<light>` in `<worldbody>` — 3 lines, makes the model render correctly out of the box in `simulate`.
- `<site>` per SolidWorks reference coordinate system per link. The tool already discovers these (`ReferenceCoordinateSystemNames` in [SW2URDF/URDFExport/ExportHelper.cs](SW2URDF/URDFExport/ExportHelper.cs)). Emitting extra coord systems (beyond the joint origin) as `<site>` gives users useful attachment points for free, without UI changes.

**Cameras and sensors** are harder to justify now — they'd need new UI (per-body camera placement, sensor type selection, target site/body), new `Robot`-tree fields, and CSV-schema extensions.

 The user wants to include sensors, cameras, lights, and sites in the initial MJCF implementation. These are MJCF-specific features without direct URDF equivalents, so I need to think through how each maps from SolidWorks. Lights are rendering-only elements that don't have physical meaning, and SolidWorks assemblies don't naturally expose lighting information, though it could potentially be added.

Cameras in MJCF attach to bodies, but SolidWorks cameras are viewport artifacts rather than assembly data. Sites are massless reference points that map well to SolidWorks coordinate systems and reference axes, which the tool already tracks. Sensors need attachment points and have no direct source in the current URDF tree.

The main blockers are that the UI has no fields for these features, and the Robot intermediate representation would need significant extension to store this data — which means modifying the URDF model classes, updating serialization, and handling migration. These features are also primarily valuable at runtime for reinforcement learning scenarios, so they're not critical for the initial implementation.

I'm leaning toward a pragmatic middle ground: add a default headlight to keep the scene renderable in simulate, and auto-emit sites for any SolidWorks reference coordinate systems beyond the joint origin since they're already discovered. This is low-cost and immediately useful. I'd defer sensors and cameras since they require real UI work and need to be backed by the Robot tree to survive a reload — users can always hand-edit the MJCF afterward if needed. Let me present this trade-off to the user so they can decide.

That's a clear principle and I agree — "no silent defaults" is the right call. In that case every one of these features needs explicit UI + a place to persist the choice on the `Link` / `Robot` tree (so it survives the CSV round-trip used by [SW2URDF/URDFExport/CSV/CSVImportExport.cs](SW2URDF/URDFExport/CSV/CSVImportExport.cs) and `DataContract` serialization).

Here's how each one looks under that constraint:

- **Sites** — lightest. A `<site>` is just a named frame. The tool already discovers per-link coord systems; the UI addition is a multi-select listbox per link (or a "promote to site" toggle alongside the existing "joint origin" dropdown). Small new `List<string> SiteCoordSystemNames` field on `Link`.
- **Lights** — cosmetic; minimal data (type `directional`/`spot`, `pos`, `dir`, `diffuse`). Typically one or two global lights, so a small "Lights" tab on the assembly export form with an add/remove list. Data lives on `Robot`, not `Link`.
- **Cameras** — similar to sites in that they attach to a body with a pose. Needs a list (name, target body, `pos`/`euler`, optional `fovy`/`mode`) stored per `Link` (or globally).
- **Sensors** — most complex. Sensor type (`jointpos`, `jointvel`, `actuatorfrc`, `framepos`, `touch`, …) plus target (joint name / site name / body name). Often depends on sites existing, so it's a natural dependency downstream.

Rather than bundle everything into one large change, I suggest a staged approach. Each stage is independently shippable, and each successive stage builds on the previous data model so we don't have to redo work:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  MVP["Stage 1 (current plan): URDF-equivalent MJCF, no silent defaults"]
  Sites["Stage 2: user-selected sites per link"]
  Lights["Stage 3: user-defined lights"]
  Cameras["Stage 4: user-defined cameras"]
  Sensors["Stage 5: user-defined sensors (depends on sites)"]
  MVP --> Sites --> Sensors
  MVP --> Lights
  MVP --> Cameras
```

Which staging do you want?

 The user's design philosophy is clear: no silent defaults, everything in the MJCF output should be explicitly chosen with override options. That means adding features like default lights or auto-generating sites from coordinate systems would violate that principle—the user needs to control what gets emitted, not have the tool decide for them.

So the real question is sequencing: do we ship a minimal URDF-equivalent MJCF first (no sensors, cameras, lights, or sites), then add user-driven site authoring in a follow-up with proper UI work? Or does the user want sites included in the initial change since they're the lightest addition and unlock downstream features like sensors and actuators? I should ask them directly whether they'd prefer the MVP first or bundle sites into this PR.

Good — I'll update the plan to bundle user-selected sites into the initial PR.

 I'm outlining the implementation approach: adding per-link site selection with UI controls, storing the selected coordinate system names on the Link object for persistence, integrating a coordinate system picker into the assembly export form, and updating the MJCF writer to generate site elements for the chosen systems. Now I need to update the plan document with these details.

The plan is updated. Summary of changes just made:

- **Todos**: added `sites-data-model` and `ui-sites`; renamed `mjcf-writer` scope to include site emission.
- **Writer**: emits a `<site>` per entry in `link.SiteCoordSystemNames`, using the SolidWorks coord-system transform relative to the joint frame.
- **Data model**: `Link.cs` gains a `SiteCoordSystemNames` `DataMember` list with CSV and `Clone`/`SetElement` round-trip support.
- **UI**: a new "Sites" group in the per-link property panel with a `CheckedListBox` of that link's reference coord systems (minus the one already selected as the joint origin). Populates and persists `SiteCoordSystemNames` just like `comboBoxCoordSys`.
- **MJCF sample**: now shows a `<site>` inside a body.
- **Out of scope**: cameras, lights, sensors deferred to follow-ups. Added an explicit "no silent defaults" principle.

The plan is ready. Since plan mode is still active, let me know when you'd like me to switch to agent mode and begin implementing.

# MJCF Export Handoff

Context for a new agent picking up the SolidWorks-URDF-Exporter MJCF work.

## Reference material

- Plan file (do **not** edit): `/home/emusser/.cursor/plans/mjcf_export_support_83bc63e8.plan.md`
- Previous chat transcript:
  `/home/emusser/.cursor/projects/home-emusser-src-dev-ros-solidworks-urdf-exporter/agent-transcripts/f4c3c4b1-7a0b-4190-935a-bcfbbe46e65d/f4c3c4b1-7a0b-4190-935a-bcfbbe46e65d.jsonl`
- Repo root: `/home/emusser/src/dev/ros/solidworks_urdf_exporter`

## Objective

Add a MuJoCo MJCF export path to the existing SolidWorks-to-URDF Exporter
without altering the URDF flow. All eight todos in the plan are now marked
**completed**; what remains is verification (see "Open follow-ups").

## Hard guiding principle (USER instruction, repeat verbatim)

> **No silent defaults.** Every element emitted in the MJCF must be either
> (a) a direct translation of URDF-tree data the user already authored, or
> (b) something the user explicitly opted into via `MjcfOptionsDialog` or
> the per-link Sites checklist. The compiler/option/default blocks expose
> only the knobs the dialog surfaces.

If a future change considers auto-generating something (a default `<light>`,
a guessed contact group, materials translation, etc.), push back unless the
user has explicitly approved it. Past decisions in this thread followed this
rule (e.g., sensors / cameras / lights deferred, materials only when the user
set a Color).

## Decisions the user made (won't be obvious from code alone)

1. **Dedicated "Export MJCF..." button**, not a URDF/MJCF format toggle on
   the existing URDF flow. Reason: MJCF has features (actuators, equalities,
   excludes, integrator/timestep) that have no URDF analog and would muddy the
   URDF UI.
2. **Scope = "mvp_plus_sites"**: This PR ships joints, inertial, geoms,
   assets, equalities (mimic), contact excludes, actuators, and **only** sites
   for the visual-extras family. Sensors, cameras, lights, textures, and OBJ
   meshes are explicitly deferred. Sites were included now because they are
   the lowest-cost addition and a prerequisite for later sensor work.
3. **Sites are user-selected**, never auto-emitted. The user picks them per
   link from a `CheckedListBox` of available reference coord systems,
   excluding the one already used as the joint origin. They are persisted on
   `Link.SiteCoordSystemNames` and round-trip through CSV.
4. **Sites are valid on fixed-frame links**, even though those links produce
   no `<inertial>`/`<geom>`. The save/fill calls intentionally sit outside
   the `if (!Link.isFixedFrame)` block in `AssemblyExportFormExtension.cs`.
5. **`MjcfWriter` must stay SolidWorks-agnostic.** Anything needing the CAD
   runtime (coord-system resolution, mesh export) is pre-computed in
   `ExportHelper.ExportMjcf` / `ResolveAllSites` and passed in as plain data
   (`IDictionary<string,List<MjcfSite>>`, `IDictionary<string,string>`). This
   is what allows `TestMjcfWriter` to run without SolidWorks installed.

## Subtle implementation notes worth knowing

- **Mesh filename flow.** `ExportHelperMjcf` writes STLs into the MJCF
  package's `meshes/` dir using a basename only, populates a
  `linkName -> basename` dictionary, and updates each `Link.Visual.Geometry.Mesh.Filename`.
  `MjcfWriter` resolves the basename against `<compiler meshdir="...">`.
  If the dictionary is missing an entry, the writer falls back to
  `link.Visual.Geometry.Mesh.Filename` (also basename-only) and finally to
  `SanitizeName(link.Name) + ".STL"`.
- **Site name normalization.** `ExportHelperMjcf.StripComponentSuffix` strips
  the SolidWorks `"<component>"` suffix from coord-system names. Duplicate
  bare names are disambiguated by appending `_2`, `_3`, ... in
  `ResolveSitesForLink`. Final names are then run through
  `MjcfWriter.SanitizeName`.
- **Quaternion convention.** `MjcfWriter.RpyToQuat` converts URDF extrinsic
  XYZ RPY (= intrinsic ZYX) into MuJoCo's default `[w,x,y,z]` quat. Used for
  body, inertial, geom, and site rotations. Don't change this without also
  updating tests; both an identity and a pure-roll case are pinned in
  `TestMjcfWriter`.
- **Planar joints** are approximated as two orthogonal `<slide>` joints in
  the plane normal to the URDF axis, named `{joint}_x` and `{joint}_y`.
  MuJoCo has no first-class planar primitive.
- **Floating base** must be the *root*; MJCF requires the free joint at the
  top body. The writer handles `link.Joint.Type == "floating"` specially
  when `isRoot=true`.
- **Mimic equality polycoef.** Encoded as `"offset multiplier 0 0 0"` so
  MJCF evaluates `dependent = multiplier*source + offset`. This is verified
  in `TestMjcfWriter.MimicJoint_EmitsEqualityConstraint_WhenOptedIn`.
- **CSV round-trip.** `Link.SiteCoordSystemNames` is serialized as a single
  semicolon-joined string under the column "Site Coord Systems"
  (`URDFExport/CSV/ContextToColumns.cs`). This matches the existing
  `SWComponents` convention so the plain `StringDictionary` reader keeps
  working.
- **UI is built programmatically.** `AssemblyExportFormMjcf.cs` and
  `MjcfOptionsDialog.cs` create their controls in code rather than via a
  `.Designer.cs` so we don't have to touch the Designer-managed layout of
  the existing form. The Sites groupbox is positioned by shrinking
  `treeViewLinkProperties` to make room. If a Designer round-trip ever runs
  on `AssemblyExportForm.Designer.cs`, double-check no programmatic controls
  were stomped.

## Files actually changed in this session

(For context only; the diff itself is the source of truth.)

- New: `SW2URDF/MJCF/MjcfWriter.cs`, `MjcfOptions.cs`, `MjcfPackage.cs`,
  `MjcfSite.cs`
- New: `SW2URDF/URDFExport/ExportHelperMjcf.cs` (partial of `ExportHelper`)
- New: `SW2URDF/UI/AssemblyExportFormMjcf.cs` (partial of
  `AssemblyExportForm`), `SW2URDF/UI/MjcfOptionsDialog.cs`
- New: `SW2URDF/Test/TestMjcfWriter.cs`
- Modified: `SW2URDF/URDF/Link.cs` (added `SiteCoordSystemNames`),
  `SW2URDF/URDFExport/CSV/ContextToColumns.cs`,
  `SW2URDF/UI/AssemblyExportForm.cs` (calls `InitializeMjcfUi`),
  `SW2URDF/UI/AssemblyExportFormExtension.cs` (Save/Fill site hooks),
  `SW2URDF/Test/TestExportHelper.cs` (`TestExportMjcf` theory),
  `SW2URDF/SW2URDF.csproj` (Compile entries)

## Open follow-ups (NOT done in this session)

1. **Build verification on Windows.** This session ran on Linux; the project
   targets `.NET Framework v4.5.2` and references SolidWorks interop DLLs.
   Nobody has actually compiled the new code. First task for the next
   session should be running an MSBuild on a Windows host with SolidWorks
   installed and triaging any compile errors.
2. **Manual MJCF validation** with the bundled assemblies (`3_DOF_ARM`,
   `4_WHEELER`, `ORIGINAL_3_DOF_ARM`): export, then open the produced `.xml`
   in `simulate` and / or `mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path()`. The plan
   explicitly calls this out under "Testing".
3. **`TestExportMjcf` is integration-level**: it spins up SolidWorks via
   the `SWTestFixture`. Make sure CI (if any) still has the SW Test
   collection. The pure unit tests in `TestMjcfWriter` are deliberately
   *not* in the SW collection and *do not* take a `SWTestFixture`; they
   should run on any machine.
4. **Future PRs (out of scope here)**: sensors, cameras, lights, material /
   texture translation, OBJ mesh export. Each of these must come with its
   own UI opt-in to honor the no-silent-defaults rule.

## How sites flow end to end (one-liner per stage)

1. UI (`AssemblyExportFormMjcf.FillSitesForLink`) populates a checklist from
   `helper.GetRefCoordinateSystems()` minus the joint coord system.
2. `SaveSitesForLink` writes checked names to `link.SiteCoordSystemNames`.
3. `ExportHelperMjcf.ResolveSitesForLink` looks up each name via
   `GetCoordinateSystemTransform`, transforms global → link-local using the
   link's joint coord system, returns `MjcfSite` objects.
4. `MjcfWriter.WriteSites` consumes the per-link list and emits `<site>`
   under each `<body>`.

## Things to avoid

- Don't add anything to `<default>`, `<option>`, `<compiler>`, etc. that the
  user hasn't exposed in `MjcfOptionsDialog`.
- Don't auto-emit `<light>` / `<camera>` / `<sensor>` / `<keyframe>`.
- Don't add textures or materials beyond the `rgba` translation already in
  `MjcfWriter.WriteVisualColor` (which only fires when the user actually set
  a color).
- Don't change `Link.Clone()` semantics without re-checking
  `SiteCoordSystemNames` is deep-copied (it currently is, in
  `Link.SetSWComponents`).
- Don't reintroduce SolidWorks types in `MjcfWriter.cs`; the testability
  story depends on that file staying CAD-free.
